context: Al-Qari’ah is early Makkan, from the first years when the Quran’s task was to break open a closed imagination. Quraysh could not conceive of the world ending or of standing before Allah, so surahs like this one arrived as controlled detonations, short, rhythmic, unforgettable. It opens with a name of the Last Day never used before, al-qari’ah, the striking knocker, repeated like a fist on a door, then twice asks the question that humbles all claimed knowledge: what will make you know what it is.

For the Prophet’s ﷺ first listeners, the surah replaced their two anchors of permanence, crowds and mountains, with images of weightlessness: mankind like moths scattered around light, mountains like carded wool drifting apart. Then it introduced the instrument that would shape Muslim conscience forever, al-mawazin, the scales, and taught the community that eternity splits along a line as fine as a weight tipping: heavy, a pleasing life; light, a mother named the abyss.
name_story: The surah is named for al-qari’ah, the Striker, the calamity that knocks and pounds, one of the proper names of the Day of Resurrection. The surah takes its title from the Day itself, and repeats the name three times at its head the way a knock repeats.

movements.h: A name repeated like a knock
movements.note: Al-Qari’ah, what is al-Qari’ah, and what will make you know what al-Qari’ah is: the Day is introduced by name, question, and awed refusal to be summarized.
The two symbols of solidity dissolve: mankind like scattered moths around a flame, and the mountains like loosened, carded wool.
The scales decide everything: whoever’s weights are heavy enters a well-pleasing life, and whoever’s are light, his mother is hawiyah, the abyss that receives him.
The surah’s question returns one last time, what will make you know what she is, and answers with two words: a raging fire.

themes.d: Al-Qari’ah joins al-Haqqah and al-Ghashiyah in the Quran’s roll of names for the Day, each name a different sound of its arrival; this one is the knock.
Crowds scatter like moths, mountains drift like wool. Everything that looks permanent is on loan, including the ground under the proud.
Mawazin, weighings: deeds have mass, and eternity turns on which pan drops, a physics of justice no one escapes and no one can bribe.
Ummuhu hawiyah: the fire is named his mother, the terrible tenderness of a refuge that consumes, for the one who made nothing else his refuge.

heart: Al-Qari’ah works on the reciter through sound before sense: the knocking name, the rhymes that fall like strokes, the question repeated until the listener admits he does not know. Slowly read, it performs a strange reversal of scale. The things that dominate your week, crowds of people and immovable circumstances, are shown scattering like moths and drifting like wool, while the things you dismiss as weightless, a small sincerity, a private sin, are revealed as the only objects with mass. The surah is a recalibration of what is heavy.

Its most piercing line is the gentlest-sounding one: fa-ummuhu hawiyah, his mother is the abyss. The scholars heard in it the image of a child running to be held, and finding that the only embrace left is the fall. Whoever recites that verse slowly finds himself checking, honestly, what he runs to when he is afraid, because that, in the end, is his mother or his abyss.

passages.why: The Day’s first image: all of mankind, every rank and tribe, scattered like moths around light.
The verse of the heavy scale: hear the only wealth that keeps its weight on that Day.
The most quietly devastating verse in the surah: the abyss as a mother’s lap for the one whose weights were light.

connections.why: Az-Zalzalah supplies the atoms, this surah supplies the scales: two halves of one courtroom.
Al-Haqqah opens with the same architecture, a name of the Day, the question, and the refrain, what will make you know.

virtue.text: No authentic hadith singles out Al-Qari’ah with a recitation reward, and it asks for none: it is one of the surahs that made the early Muslims’ hair grey with the vividness of the Day, and that vividness is its gift to the reciter.
